South Korean chipmaker SK Hynix plunged over 8%, while Samsung Electronics shed 7%. LG Innotek and LG Display fell 10% and 7.7%, respectively, as selling pressure spread across the country's technology sector.
The rout came as investors worried that Democrats' sweeping victory in the U.S. midterm elections could lead to tighter restrictions on data-center development, potentially slowing demand for AI chips and related infrastructure.
In Japan, semiconductor-related stocks also fell, with chip-testing equipment maker Advantest plunging 12.2%, while Tokyo Electron slid 7.3%. Technology investment giant SoftBank Group tumbled 11.6%.
Shares of memory chipmaker Kioxia Holdings fell nearly 10%, while Renesas Electronics declined 7.5%.
In Taiwan, semiconductor stocks also came under heavy selling pressure, with contract chipmaker TSMC sliding 9.6%. Electronics manufacturers Hon Hai Precision Industry, also known as Foxconn, and Foxconn Technology fell 9.4% and 9.1%, respectively, as the regional technology rout deepened.
China was also caught in the regional sell-off, with the tech-heavy STAR Market and the ChiNext Artificial Intelligence Index both tumbling more than 4%.
The declines followed a brutal session on Wall Street, where the Nasdaq Composite sank 5.5%, amid mounting concerns over the sustainability of the AI investment boom and returns on massive data-center spending. It closed more than 10% below its recent peak. The Philadelphia Semiconductor Index plunged 12.2%.
The sell-off in Asian equities has been exacerbated by investors unwinding positions, stop-loss selling and heightened volatility, Timothy Moe, chief Asia Pacific equity strategist at Goldman Sachs, told CNBC's "Squawk Box Asia" on Friday.
He added that potential political opposition to U.S. data center construction may affect demand and profits for Asian AI hardware suppliers.
"If there's concern about the speed and magnitude of buildout in the U.S., then obviously that's going to put all that into question," he said. "The market's tendency is always to shoot first and ask questions later. I think that's exactly what's happening now."

title: The engine parts that 'fight the laws of the universe'
titleJa: The engine parts that 'fight the laws of the universe'
summaryJa: Investment has surged into the making of jet turbine blades - an extremely difficult component to make.
bodyOriginal:
The engine parts that 'fight the laws of the universe'
- Published
Every time you fly, an extraordinary feat of endurance occurs inside the aircraft's engines.
Hidden from view inside the sleek outer nacelle are hundreds of little turbine blades that can shrug off enormous mechanical stresses and temperatures exceeding 1,500C.
It is a true engineering marvel. And these hardy blades are not sculpted or cut from their material – they are grown.
During the 1960s, engineers worked out how to take a molten metal alloy, cast it into the shape of a turbine blade, and then cool it very carefully from one end to the other over a matter of hours. A single crystal or grain of metal alloy forms during this process of gradual, delicate solidification.
Like turning a cup of water into one big snowflake, of your own design, rather than a mini blizzard of many smaller snowflakes.
"It's about as complicated as manufacturing gets," says Ben Fifoot, manufacturing engineer at Rolls-Royce, which makes turbine blades in the UK. "It's a real motivator to get out of bed in the morning."
Only a handful of companies around the world can produce these single crystal turbine blades, and the process has been perfected end-to-end in just five countries, including the US and UK. Engine-makers continually vie for access to the technology.
Rolls-Royce, GE and France's Safran are among the few firms that have perfected the process.
In September, GE Aerospace announced, external it would acquire its turbine blade supplier for $11.75bn (£8.78bn). Neither company responded to BBC News' requests for comment but the move has been described as an effort to ensure supply of these critical components.
Separately, in March, Rolls-Royce said it would invest more than £19m in its Rotherham blade casting facility.
Turbine blade specialists continue to work on improving the capabilities of this little-known technology. All the while, China is desperate to prove that its engineers can produce turbine blades of the same quality as those in the West. Who will come out on top?
"Demand for [turbine blades] is huge. So few companies have managed to do it, which does give it this kind of magical aura," says Bill Sweetman, an aviation industry writer and consultant.
He suspects GE Aerospace's recent move is about securing reliability and predictability in the notoriously volatile aircraft manufacturing supply chain.
But why is the single crystal casting process, which has been around for decades now, still so specialist?
To grow one of these blades, asserts Fifoot, is to "fight the laws of the universe".
This is because each molten blade would naturally cool into a solid object consisting of many small grains of metal alloy, all jumbled together. But you don't want a crumbly sugar cube, you want a perfect diamond.
Getting a single crystal to grow into the shape of the blade instead isn't just a matter of cooling the molten version down slowly, the process also uses a bizarre trick called a pigtail.
The pigtail is a small spiral at one end of the blade. Fifoot says that, at the beginning of the cooling process, this spiral "chokes" the flow of solidifying crystals so that just one takes over. A bit like a hairpin corner in an F1 race right before the finish line – one driver can take the lead here and go on to win.
"Sometimes we need to play around with the number of turns or the angles on [the pigtail] to try and get more favourable grain," adds Fifoot. Once the blade is formed, this crucial but sacrificial spiral is cut off.
Blades made by Rolls-Royce are used in aircraft engines including the Trent XWB-84, which powers the Airbus A350-900, and the Trent 1000 XE, for the Boeing 787.
The single crystal is essential to ensure each blade's performance. Sometimes a blade doesn't cool quite as planned, for example two crystals form within it instead of just one, and the metal alloy must be reprocessed so that the manufacturer may re-use the material.
Special ceramic coatings also protect blades from extreme temperatures inside engines. And another important feature is that blades are cast with tiny channels that allow a flow of cooler air to coat them in a kind of film while the aircraft engine is working.
"The drive at the moment [across the industry] is currently to make those cooling passages really intricate," says Paul Withey, at the University of Birmingham, who formerly worked for Rolls-Royce. The more turbulent those little flows of cool air are, he explains, the more they will knock heat out of the surrounding, much hotter air.
And blade-makers also seek to reduce the mass of these components as much as possible.
"If we can take any weight out of it, you can run that engine more efficiently using less fuel – you can spin it faster and hotter," says Fifoot.
Meanwhile, China hopes to become only the sixth country to master the whole technology chain for single crystal blade casting.
A report in May, external quoted one engineer at the AECC Beijing Institute of Aeronautical Materials claiming that China now had a single crystal alloy "superior to or equivalent to the second-generation single-crystal superalloys widely used in Europe and the US". It costs less to make, too, apparently.
But the West has a "huge advantage" over China given that the majority of commercial airliner production happens there, says Sweetman. Supply chains and the latest innovations are generally clustered in the West. Plus, Western manufacturers also have lengthy safety records under their belts.
China must compete on practically every aspect of aircraft manufacturing, external – by no means just on turbine blades – in order to make serious in-roads. "You can definitely see that happening but it's a long, uphill struggle," adds Sweetman.
Demand for aircraft is currently high, which is already straining various supply chains in the industry. That demand could grow higher still, suggests Withey.
During the next few years, one of the two main aircraft manufacturers, Airbus and Boeing, could launch a new short-haul plane, external, he says. Then, the other would have to follow suit in order to remain competitive.
"There'll be a bun fight," says Withey, over who gets to supply the engines and, by extension, those all-important single crystal turbine blades.

title: 'I was asked if I was a crier': Your worst job interviews revealed
titleJa: 'I was asked if I was a crier': Your worst job interviews revealed
summaryJa: Bad job interviews can be horrible to experience in the moment, but there is a lot they can teach us about the world of work
bodyOriginal:
'I was asked if I was a crier': Your worst job interviews revealed
- Published
Tiara Allen arrived on time to interview for a retail job. Her interviewer didn't.
She waited for around 40 minutes in a shopping centre while the interviewer's co-worker called them "two or three times".
When they finally showed up, Tiara says she was told it was because the meeting wasn't in the schedule.
She needed work at the time, so took the job when she was offered it, but says she would handle the situation differently now.
"I would not take a job if they took that long," she says, adding that she believed her treatment during the interview was a sign of how the firm tended to treat staff.
Tiara is far from alone. She is one of many people who spoke to the BBC about their worst job interview experiences after we wrote about the one interview question that leaves you feeling uncomfortable.
While those situations can be hard to deal with in the moment, they can also teach us a lot about the world of work.
'Are you a crier?'
During an interview for an assistant at a book publisher in New York, Chas Edwards was asked a question he wasn't expecting.
"I was asked for my first job if I was a crier," he recalls.
Thinking the interviewer was being funny, Chas replied that he didn't cry. He was later told that this was why he got the job.
"Her last assistant had cried – too often, I guess? – and she wanted someone who didn't cry. So she was being serious and I thought it was a joke," he says.
It was a bad sign. Chas says it was "a terrible, terrible job with a miserable boss" and while he managed to make it through 13 months there without crying he was "crying inside".
"I set the world record for working for this person. No-one had ever lasted three months with her before," he recalls.
Despite all this, Chas says he is in some ways grateful the experience was so awful.
"Because every job since then, even the bad ones, are not that bad," he says, adding that he can "cry anywhere now".
Corinne Card also found herself floored when the first question she was asked in an interview for an administrative job was if she liked working with people.
When she replied yes, she was told that the job wouldn't be for her and the interview ended there.
"I don't know if it was a deliberate trap. Because who would answer 'I don't like working with people'?"
Corinne Mills, joint managing director of Personal Career Management, says that it can be worth asking an interviewer to clarify any weird questions, perhaps by repeating the question back to them.
However, if a line of questioning is really off-putting, she says it can also be a sign of what it's like to work there, saying that interviews are also about candidates judging the company.
Meanwhile, other questions are not just annoying – they are illegal.
Discrimination against a protected characteristic is against the law, external, meaning an employer cannot treat you less favourably based on your age, disability, gender reassignment, marriage, pregnancy, race, religion, sex, or sexual orientation.
Employment lawyer Roy Magara says that women being asked if they intend on having children in an interview is a "quite common" kind of bias. He says he has also seen a case where an older candidate was told he didn't get the job after an interview because he didn't fit the "vibe" of a younger team.
If you think these sorts of biases took place in your interview, Roy says you can send the company a subject access request, external to see how they discussed your application internally.
Worst-case scenarios like these can make interviews feel very difficult, especially considering the control employers have over candidates.
Euan Cameron, co-founder of hiring software Willo, says that even with this power imbalance it's important not to overthink what an interview is.
"An interview is just a conversation between two people," he says.
Of course, as in Tiara's case, it helps when both of those people show up.

A trader works on the floor of the New York Stock Exchange (NYSE) at the opening bell in New York City on November 4, 2026.
Timothy A. Clary | Afp | Getty Images
Stocks suffered a major sell-off on Thursday as investors' fears about a slowdown in the buildout of artificial intelligence rocked not only the trade itself but also the broader market.
The tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite receded more than 5% and finished in correction territory alongside the small-cap Russell 2000 index. The blue-chip Dow Jones Industrial Average retreated more than 1,800 points, or more than 3%, and the broad market S&P 500 pulled back more than 4%.
Those moves gave back the big gains seen in Wednesday's postelection rally and then some.
Here are the most breathtaking statistics from the day's rout:
- The Nasdaq Composite posted its worst performance in a single day since April 4, 2025, when it fell 5.82%
- The S&P 500 notched its worst single-day performance since April 4, 2025, when it declined 5.97%
- The Dow Jones Industrial Average secured its worst day since April 4, 2025, when it dropped more than 2,200 points, or 5.5%
- The "Magnificent Seven" lost more than $1 trillion in aggregate market cap, with Nvidia leading the way at a loss of more than $440 billion
- Nvidia fell more than 9% and turned negative on the year, with its year-to-date fall now at 2.6%
- The CBOE Volatility Index (VIX) — which hit its highest level since March 31 — gained 11.57 points for the biggest point gain since April 4, 2025, when the VIX gained 15.29 points
- On the New York Stock Exchange, declining stocks outpaced advancing stocks 2,344 to 416, or almost 6 to 1
- On the Nasdaq Composite, declining stocks outpaced advancing stocks 4,166 to 855, or almost 5 to 1
- All 11 S&P 500 sectors were negative, led to the downside by information technology, down 7.30% to post its worst daily performance since March 16, 2020, when it fell 13.92%
- Industrials fell 4.12%, its worst daily performance since April 4, 2025, when it fell 6.29%
- The Technology Select Sector SPDR Fund (XLK) fell 8.04%, turning in the worst daily performance since March 16, 2020, when the XLK fell 13.81%
- The XLK traded more than 33 million shares, more than three times the 30-day average volume of 9.2 million shares
- 174, or 34.6%, of stocks in the S&P 500 are 20% or more below the 52-week high, including SanDisk, Intel, Marvell Technology, Seagate Technology, Coinbase, Lumentum, Oracle, On Semiconductor, Micron Technology, Caterpillar, Robinhood, Alphabet, Nvidia, Lululemon
- 310, or 61.6%, of stocks in the S&P 500 are 10% or more below the 52-week high
- 59, or 58.4%, of stocks in the Nasdaq-100 are more than 20% off the 52-week high, including Rocket Lab, CoreWeave, Arm Holdings and SpaceX, among others
- 72, or 71.3%, of stocks in the Nasdaq-100 are more than 10% off the 52-week high

title: Firms told to publish salaries in job adverts ahead of new law
titleJa: Firms told to publish salaries in job adverts ahead of new law
summaryJa: The government argues the change will help jobseekers and could help to prevent pay discrimination.
bodyOriginal:
Firms told to publish salaries in job adverts ahead of new law
- Published
Businesses should publish salaries in job adverts now, Prime Minister Andy Burnham is telling firms, rather than wait for a new law to come in that will force them to do so.
The government is planning to make pay details compulsory in adverts, with legislation on the issue being brought forward "as soon as possible".
It argues the change will help jobseekers, particularly those applying for their first job, and could help prevent pay discrimination. However, one industry group said setting pay was a complex process and regulating adverts was not always suitable.
It comes a week after the UK's equality watchdog said employees should legally be able to find out what their colleagues are earning.
Greater transparency
The Cabinet Office launched a consultation into pay and reducing discrimination in the summer, and the government said there had been "overwhelming support" for greater transparency, with 94% of respondents backing the move.
"Whether you're a young person starting out or a parent trying to support your family, you should know what a job pays before spending your time and effort applying for it," Burnham said.
The government said the move was part of attempts to reduce the nearly one million young people not in education, employment or training - or "Neet" - ahead of the final report of the Milburn Review into youth inactivity, which is due in the coming weeks.
Publishing salary details upfront could "expose unjustified differences in pay, give workers greater confidence to challenge discrimination and prevent disagreements over pay escalating into disputes".
The proposals are similar to measures being introduced in the European Union., external
Employers in Europe will have to disclose the initial pay or range for new roles, which must either be included in a published job advert or shared before an interview.
According to data from UK jobs website Adzuna, external, 51% of the adverts on its site in September had salary information, but the proportion has been falling in recent years.
Adzuna co-founder Andrew Hunter said being open about pay "should be the norm, not the exception".
He added that employers who put a salary on a job advert "attract more applicants, and better-suited ones".
'More complicated'
Previous research from the CIPD, external, an industry body for human resources managers, has indicated that the public sector and charities are more likely to reveal pay information that private firms, while pay ranges were more common than specific salaries.
But it found not all employers were "fully transparent", with pay ranges sometimes wider than £10,000.
CIPD chief executive Neil Carberry said that while, in principle, giving salary details was "a good thing", in practice it was "more complicated".
"There isn't always a single fixed figure, and employers will want to set pay based on a candidate's skills, experience and potential."
Carberry added the process was complex, saying that drafting job adverts is "best left to good employer practice rather than government regulation".
The government has said it will set out further details on what information will be required and how the legislation will be enforced "in due course".
Last week, the Equality and Human Rights Commission (EHRC), said publishing salaries in job adverts would be a "positive step".
It also said bosses should be required to respond to questionnaires about colleagues' pay to cut pay discrimination.
At present, employers do not have to respond to employee requests for salary information about their co-workers.
The EHRC also said employers should be prevented from asking about current salary when offering a job to stop a history of discrimination from continuing.
Employers in the UK are currently allowed to ask you how much you get paid in your current role, but applicants are under no obligation to tell them.

The Cabinet Office launched a consultation into pay and reducing discrimination in the summer, and the government said there had been "overwhelming support" for greater transparency, with 94% of respondents backing the move.

The government said the move was part of attempts to reduce the nearly one million young people not in education, employment or training - or "Neet" - ahead of the final report of the Milburn Review into youth inactivity, which is due in the coming weeks.
Publishing salary details upfront could "expose unjustified differences in pay, give workers greater confidence to challenge discrimination and prevent disagreements over pay escalating into disputes".
The proposals are similar to measures being introduced in the European Union., external
Employers in Europe will have to disclose the initial pay or range for new roles, which must either be included in a published job advert or shared before an interview.

Previous research from the CIPD, external, an industry body for human resources managers, has indicated that the public sector and charities are more likely to reveal pay information that private firms, while pay ranges were more common than specific salaries.

Last week, the Equality and Human Rights Commission (EHRC), said publishing salaries in job adverts would be a "positive step".
It also said bosses should be required to respond to questionnaires about colleagues' pay to cut pay discrimination.
At present, employers do not have to respond to employee requests for salary information about their co-workers.
The EHRC also said employers should be prevented from asking about current salary when offering a job to stop a history of discrimination from continuing.

title: Wall Street's fear gauge surges the most since April. Why traders think it should be even higher
titleJa: Wall Street's fear gauge surges the most since April. Why traders think it should be even higher
summaryJa: From its intraday low to high Thursday, VIX moved more than 11 points, the biggest one-day move since April 9.
bodyOriginal:
Whether it's a referendum on the midterms or just a continuation of a bear market in semiconductors that dates back to the group's peak in June, one thing's clear from the options action Thursday: few traders saw this coming.
That's evident in the surge in Cboe Volatility index (VIX), which jumped as much as 5.7 points to above 28 about 90 minutes after the opening bell on Thursday. It's the highest reading on VIX since March 31, the day after the S&P 500 bottomed after selling off as tensions between Iran, Israel and the U.S. reached fever pitch.
From its intraday low to high Thursday, VIX moved more than 11 points, the biggest one-day move since April 9. Yet with the S&P 500 down 3%, there's an argument to be made that volatility should be higher. Traders use a rule of thumb that 16 points for the VIX equate to a 1% move in the index.
The S&P 500 was headed for its worst decline since April 2025.
"My data says to de-risk, but my gut says this is a blowout that could create a dip-buying opportunity" said Noel Smith, "I do not see macro stuff causing this, like oil or rates. Those things are relatively unchanged. The tape looks like a liquidation and that's exactly what it is according to what I'm hearing with regards to a hedge fund."
Looking at Wednesday's response to the selloff in semiconductors adds a wrinkle for traders that pointed to a too-calm VIX despite Wednesday's tech-stock wreck. With the VanEck Semiconductor ETF down 3%, it was the first day in market history that the VIX concurrently fell more than 4 points, according to data from the X account "OddStats."
As of midday, nearly 800,000 calls traded on the VIX, 3.5 times higher than 30-day average, according to Cboe data.

title: Trump's energy deals are about to face a wave of investigations by Democrats
titleJa: Trump's energy deals are about to face a wave of investigations by Democrats
summaryJa: Democrats are certain to scrutinize the U.S. intervention in Venezuela, administration mineral deals and the cancellation of previously funded energy projects.
bodyOriginal:
President Donald Trump is expected to face a wave of investigations when Democrats take control of Congress in January. His sweeping deal-making in the energy sector is likely to become a central focus.
Democrats have pressed the White House for months on the legality of its intervention in Venezuela's oil sector and its cancellation of renewable energy projects funded by the Biden administration. They have raised conflict of interest concerns over numerous deals in the minerals sector.
But, until now, the opposition party could do little more than send strongly worded letters to administration officials. When the next Congress convenes in January, the Democrats will wield the subpoena power that comes with committee control, giving them the authority to compel testimony and the disclosure of documents.
The House Energy and Commerce Committee in the next Congress intends to pursue an aggressive oversight agenda to root out corruption, Rep. Frank Pallone, the New Jersey Democrat who will likely chair the panel, said in a statement.
With comfortable majorities in the House and Senate, Democrats will likely pass a war powers resolution that demands an end to the conflict, which has hiked fuel prices in the U.S. and around the world.
1. Iran war
Crude oil prices sold off sharply Wednesday as the market expected the election defeat to push Trump to cut a deal with Iran. Vice President JD Vance blamed the Republican loss directly on the war, raising questions about whether there is support inside the administration to continue the conflict.
House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, who will likely take over the House speaker's gavel in January, said Wednesday that Democrats will "end this reckless and costly war of choice that has skyrocketed gas prices all across the country."
The new Congress will try to rein in the administration by passing legislation to stop the conflict, said Rep. Ted Lieu, vice chairman of the Democratic caucus. Jeffries has said Democrats will pass a war powers resolution, though Trump will almost certainly wield his veto. It is unclear whether Democrats will try to restrict funding for the war as well.
Nevertheless, tumbling crude prices could push gasoline below $4 per gallon in the next week and diesel under $6 by Thanksgiving, said Patrick De Haan, head of petroleum analysis at GasBuddy, in a social media post Wednesday.
But the odds still favor military escalation in the Middle East, warned Bob McNally, president of Rapidan Energy and a former energy advisor to President George W. Bush.
"Iran is hardened in its uncompromising position," McNally said. "Trump, having now paid a huge price for his determination to prevent Iran from obtaining a nuclear weapon, is unlikely to let go of this legacy goal and walk away."
2. Venezuela's oil
Democratic lawmakers have pressed the Trump administration for months to provide Congress with an accounting of how Venezuela's oil revenues have been spent — to no avail.
Washington seized control of Venezuela's oil exports in January after ousting former President Nicolás Maduro in a military raid. The Pentagon took a stake in an obscure oil company, North American Blue Energy Partners, or NABEP, that is supposed to develop Venezuelan oil reserves. The deal supposedly gives the U.S. control over 65 billion barrels of oil.
Democratic House members warned the oil industry in January that entering into an agreement with the U.S. on Venezuelan oil could expose the industry to "legal risk, including civil liability from creditors who hold nearly $200 billion worth of debt to Venezuela and their various state-owned entities."
Democratic senators subsequently sent a letter in September to Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth and Energy Secretary Chris Wright questioning the legal basis for the U.S. government's deal with NABEP.
Energy analysts warned when the NABEP deal was announced in August that it might not survive if Democrats take power in Washington.
3. Deals for critical minerals
Democrats have also raised conflict of interest concerns over the Trump administration's series of deals in the critical minerals sector.
The White House has justified the deals, often involving government equity stakes in private companies, as necessary to support a segment of the mining industry that's critical to U.S. national security and that has been undercut by competitors in China.
But Democratic senators have pointed to the involvement of Cantor Fitzgerald in a number of those deals as cause for concern. Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick ran Cantor before joining the Trump administration. He personally divested from Cantor after joining the Cabinet and turned over control to his sons.
The Democratic senators demanded in a July letter that the federal government preserve any records related to deals involving 14 companies.
For his part, the Commerce secretary dismissed the allegations. "If the Democrats send me letters, I will respond to the letters but they don't matter, since when you do nothing wrong, you don't worry about it and you don't care," Lutnick told CNBC in a September interview.
"You just answer their silly questions and you move on," Lutnick said. "This is a waste of time trying to create something that doesn't exist."
Others are less cavalier. USA Rare Earth, one of the companies named in the senators' letter, has warned investors that its deal making the U.S. government one of its stockholders has few precedents.
As a consequence, the company could be subject to litigation, political scrutiny and a change in federal priorities, it said in a March filing with the Securities and Exchange Commission.
4. Canceled energy projects
The Trump administration has favored fossil fuels and waged a relentless campaign against renewable energy, particularly wind power, since taking office.
Democrats are unlikely to restore tax credits phased out by Trump's big tax bill due to the president's veto power. But they are certain to press the administration on the nearly $8 billion of energy projects it has canceled in states that supported Vice President Kamala Harris in the 2024 presidential election.
Energy Secretary Chris Wright has told Congress that the projects were not canceled based on political considerations. Several House Democrats have accused Wright of giving false testimony, an allegation the Energy Department has denied.
Democrats are also scrutinizing the administration's efforts to kill offshore wind power in the U.S. The Interior Department has tried to buy out leases for several such projects, for example, paying TotalEnergies nearly $1 billion to cancel an offshore wind project and stop investing in any similar projects in the U.S. in the future. Total agreed to invest in natural gas instead.
Reps. Jared Huffman and Jamie Raskin, the ranking Democrats on the natural resources and judiciary committees, respectively, called the TotalEnergies deal unlawful and launched an investigation in April.

title: Shares in Musk's SpaceX plunge as tech and AI stocks fall
titleJa: Shares in Musk's SpaceX plunge as tech and AI stocks fall
summaryJa: The market has been reacting to possible tougher scrutiny of data centre construction and the AI industry following the US mid-terms
bodyOriginal:
Shares in Musk's SpaceX plunge as tech and AI stocks fall
- Published
Shares in Elon Musk's SpaceX have plunged as tech and artificial intelligence stocks more broadly plummeted a day after the Democrats swept to victory in the midterms.
Those losses dragged the tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite stock index down, which had fallen by more than 5% at one point in early trading.
The market has been reacting to possible tougher scrutiny of data centre construction and the artificial intelligence (AI) industry following Democrat wins in key data centre states including Texas.
Following the election, some tech leaders have acknowledged they need to improve their communication around data centres and the benefits of AI.
SpaceX shares were down more than 9% in by lunchtime in Thursday trading, while Tesla shares dropped more than 11%.
Musk had spent nearly $450m backing Republican campaigns, including at least $45m in support of Ken Paxton for the Texas senate seat, but Texas was turned blue in the Democratic tsunami on Tuesday night.
Texas governor-elect Gina Hinojosa campaigned heavily against data centres, pledging a moratorium on new construction in the sector.
Shares in chipmakers have been suffering, with AMD dropping more than 14% on Thursday, while Micron shares had dropped by as much as 17% before recovering slightly.
Intel shares are down by more than 7% and shares in Nvidia have fallen nearly 9%, while the Philadelphia Semiconductor Index had fallen by 10%.
The stock falls also hit the S&P 500 index, which dropped by 3.8% by lunchtime.
Susannah Streeter, chief investment strategist at Wealth Club, said the steep sell-off on the Nasdaq and the S&P 500 was sending shockwaves into other markets.
"Fresh panic over the AI trade has hit Wall Street hard," she said.
"Fears that the vast sums poured into AI infrastructure may not deliver the returns investors have been banking on are now colliding with the prospect of a sharp slowdown in data centre construction."
Some tech leaders have said they were caught off guard by the backlash against data centres in the midterms.
OpenAI president and co-founder Greg Brockman said he believed everyone had been surprised by the reaction to data centres, and more work needed to be done to ensure communities were on board.
"A lot of our shift over the course of this year has really been to realise that from San Francisco trying to build infrastructure in Texas, Georgia, and other places, you can't just tweet and say: 'This is going to be good.' You need to be in those communities," Brockman said at the WSJ Tech conference in Napa, California on Wednesday evening.
Meta's president Dina Powell McCormick agreed that the industry needed to improve their communication about the benefits of AI.
"I think we need to double and triple down on telling the story," she told the WSJ conference.
Alongside the immediate impacts of the US mid-term elections, some investors have become concerned that AI shares could be in a bubble that is due a correction.

title: Drunk and dangerous e-bike riders face on-the-spot fines under crackdown
titleJa: Drunk and dangerous e-bike riders face on-the-spot fines under crackdown
summaryJa: A consultation will consider fines and other ways to clamp down on dangerous e-bike riders.
bodyOriginal:
Drunk and dangerous e-bike riders face on-the-spot fines under crackdown
- Published
People riding drunk or dangerously on e-bikes – and those who jump red lights - could face on-the-spot fines under plans to curb anti-social behaviour.
Firms which run shared e-bike schemes will also be expected to manage their fleets better and provide designated parking areas to keep pavements safe.
They could also be required to take out insurance so people can claim compensation if they are hit by someone on a shared bike.
It's part of a crackdown on what ministers called the "wild west" of e-biking – with a patchwork of rules across the country often leaving the streets unsafe for pedestrians.
A consultation launched on Thursday sets out proposed national standards to make journeys safer for everyone and keep pavements clear, particularly for wheelchair users and families with prams.
The first e-bikes were launched in Exeter in 2016 and arrived in London a year later, growing to become a popular commuter option.
According to the Greater London Authority, 37 million trips were taken on dockless e-bikes last year – a third more than the previous year.
Shared e-bikes - such as Lime, Voi, Beryl, Dott, Forest and Bolt - make short journeys quick and convenient.
While some areas enforce rules that mean shared bikes can only be left in specific areas, others have looser rules.
Under the government's proposals, local leaders will be able to license schemes in their area, allowing them to enforce minimum standards and better integrate e-bikes into existing transport networks.
Measures could include requiring operators to have a parking plan and to manage fleet sizes and operating areas, so bikes aren't overcrowding streets.
The consultation will also consider ways to tackle antisocial and illegal behaviour, to prevent users from riding shared cycles drunk, underage, or on pavements. There will also be clear consequences set out – such as fines - for this type of behaviour.
The government is also consulting on whether local leaders should have extra powers, including setting fees and requirements for operators to share data to improve enforcement and journey planning.
The consultation will last for eight weeks after which the government will draw up legislation to implement the changes.
'Dumped e-scooters force blind people into road'
- Published1 April
Red light jumping cyclists offered film over fine
- Published14 October
'Our lives will never be the same again after Lime bike crash'
- Published29 June
Prime Minister Andy Burnham said the e-bike clampdown was a "small but important everyday fix" which would make streets safer.
Transport Secretary Heidi Alexander said the government wanted e-bike schemes to "grow in popularity" but acknowledged they were "causing a little bit of nuisance at the moment".
Asked how punishments for dangerous cycling could be enforced, Alexander said licensing rules could allow for fines but added: "What you can't do is legislate for every eventuality, you can't legislate for idiots."
"The police enforce the rules of the road to stop cyclists when they are behaving recklessly but police have got a lot on their plate so individuals have to take some responsibility," she added.
Bosses at Lime, Voi and Bolt all welcomed the proposals, adding that consistent standards being applied across the country would provide clarity and certainty for operators, riders and the general public.
Mike Wordingham from the Royal National Institute for the Blind said 92% of blind and partially sighted people had been forced to walk into roads due to e-bikes blocking pavements.
He welcomed the government's announced but warned that tackling rider behaviour would be "difficult" and said a locally-led approach shouldn't lead to "a patchwork of regulations and inconsistency in implementing them".

title: Here's what the Democratic election rout could mean for the U.S. economy
titleJa: Here's what the Democratic election rout could mean for the U.S. economy
summaryJa: The biggest forces shaping the economy aren't going to change just because the party in power did.
bodyOriginal:
The Democratic midterm election sweep could result in changes in economic policies related to trade, spending priorities and artificial intelligence. But the biggest forces shaping the economy aren't going to change just because the party in power did.
Affordability pressures, heavy levels of government spending and growth that is dependent on the artificial intelligence tail wind are likely to persist, economists say. And all of those factors pose risks to the economy.
"It's in a very kind of fragile place, and I don't know that it would take a lot to push the economy off the rails, and recession becomes a much greater risk," said Mark Zandi, chief economist at Moody's Analytics. "That isn't the case at the moment, but I don't think that's gone away."
Zandi said he had been worried before the election that the economy was under threat from inflation, an underwhelming labor market and geopolitical dangers, and remains concerned now.

Despite the various headwinds and political uncertainty, most of Wall Street expects the growth in the economy to continue — if not without hiccups and lingering issues over the cost of living.

Brusuelas also sees the opportunity to "reset" the trade agreement between the U.S., Mexico and Canada after a year and a half of tension from the Trump tariffs and reprisals.
"We only have a 15% probability of recession over the next 12 months," he said. "The outcome of the election was immaterial to that estimate."

title: Faisal Islam: How high will interest rates go?
titleJa: Faisal Islam: How high will interest rates go?
summaryJa: The BBC's economics editor views one more interest rate as likely, but thinks that will be all.
bodyOriginal:
Faisal Islam: How high will interest rates go?
- Published
Interest rates have risen to 4% and the Bank of England has indicated there are more rises to come. The question is how many? There is a split on the rate-setting committee here.
Three of the nine voting members referred to "rises" plural. One member voted for a bigger increase, to 4.25%. Three referred to just one more including governor Andrew Bailey.
My read on this is that the expectation is for one more rise in February. Two and done, but it depends.
It is painful for those on variable mortgages, but should not be seen as the start of a cycle of hikes.
Predicting where interest rates will go is like throwing darts at a board that constantly moves around the wall, with expectations of how long the Iran War will last and its impact on the economy and prices lurching from day to day.
At least there is no blindfold.
The Bank's forecasts indicate inflation is heading to just under 5% next spring as a typical household energy bill surges by 27% in January to £2,150 a year.
Why now?
Why have they raised now? High and rising inflation risks a further cycle of self fulfilling expectations of rising prices. It hasn't been seen so far, however. The war has lasted for 9 months, and led to oil prices used in the forecast averaging $108 a barrel.
And yet on the day they have announced the rate rise, the oil price is actually 13% lower than that having fallen in the run up and after the US mid term elections, reflecting expectations or guesses that President Trump will now retreat or deescalate from the Iran war.
The other notable factor is that the UK economy is performing much better than forecasts and expectations. This is underlined by the Bank of England's latest forecasts.
Growth has been 0.6%, and 0.5% in the first two quarters of the year. It is heading for 0.7%, the Bank said, between July and September, before slowing in the three months to the end of the year. Unemployment has stabilised, actually falling a little.
Some of this has fed through into a better performing currency, with sterling at its highest level since the Brexit referendum, when measured against a basket of currencies. This can help rein in inflation by making imports cheaper.
So, this is an unusual type of uncertainty. Even the expected further rise, probably in February next year is conditional on the war continuing.
The Bank of England stopped waiting for President Trump's war to end today, but perhaps the Democrats' resounding victory in the US midterm elections will stop the inflationary wave? The Bank has thrown a tentative first dart, and there is probably another to come.

title: Three ways the interest rate rise could affect you
titleJa: Three ways the interest rate rise could affect you
summaryJa: Job, loans and savings are all affected by the rise in interest rates announced by the Bank of England.
bodyOriginal:
Three ways the interest rate rise could affect you
- Published
Interest rates have been raised for the first time in more than three years - and it could be good and bad news for you.
Here are three ways the increase to 4% from 3.75% could affect you.
1. Jobs and pay
Rate-setters at the Bank make changes to interest rates to fulfil their role of keeping price rises at a steady level.
Higher rates are meant to encourage people to spend less, reducing demand for goods and services and limiting price rises.
This impacts businesses in two ways - less money to spend among their customers may mean they sell less, but also the cost of borrowing to invest as a company goes up.
Many businesses, particularly small ones, have variable rate loans which are influenced by the Bank rate.
Firms say higher rates limit their ability to offer new jobs and wage rises.
Mitchell Barnes, founder and chief executive of Ryse 3D, which manufactures 3D parts for the defence and automotive sectors, said the "reality" of rising interest rates was to look at the cost of employees and people.
That could include greater use of robots rather than workers.
"It's going to cause issues with, I suppose, employment across all sectors for people," he said.
"You're going to see reduced employment, more automation, more robotics being put into facilities, just in order to increase efficiency and make that money go further."
2. Boost to savings
The Bank rate - and where it is expected to go in future - has a significant impact on the interest rates customers are offered on savings products.
So, if you're saving up for something quite expensive, like a holiday, or very expensive, like a home, then a rate rise could be good news.
When interest rates were low throughout the 2010s, the returns for savers were poor, but borrowing costs were low too.
The answer then and now, according to experts, is to make sure you move your savings to benefit from the best possible rates.
You need £17,000 for a first home - here's how to save it
- Published28 September
Faisal Islam: How high will interest rates go?
- Published6 hours ago
Leaving your savings in an old account (a product not offered to new customers), rather than shopping around, can mean you are penalised for your loyalty.
"Savers have endured years of unrewarded loyalty, with those leaving [a £20,000 cash pot] in closed accounts losing out on an extra £139 over the past three years compared to on-sale easy access accounts," said Rachel Springall, from financial information service Moneyfacts.
She also said locking away your money for longer, with a fixed-term deal, is usually more lucrative.
The other flipside is that renting while you save could get more expensive, because a rising Bank rate may well increase costs for landlords.
3. Mortgages and loans
The big losers from a rate rise are those who borrow money, and specifically those on variable rate mortgages.
About 500,000 homeowners have a mortgage that "tracks" the Bank of England's rate.
Any rise in the Bank rate means an increase in the monthly repayments on their outstanding loan. For a typical loan, the cost is going up by about £31 a month now the Bank has raised the base rate, but it depends on the size of people's loans.
An additional 500,000 homeowners on standard variable rates (SVRs) must wait to see if their lender chooses to pass on any Bank rate rise. Typically, this would mean a £14 increase per month in repayments for a 0.25 percentage points rates rise.
If you, like 87% of mortgage-holders, have a fixed-rate deal, then the payments will stay the same until the end of your current deal, which is usually two or five years.
While monthly payments are not immediately affected by a rate change, future deals are. Lenders had already "priced in" the latest rate rise when quoting new deals. Expectations for the Bank rate into next year are crucial on what they offer next.
The average rate on fixed deals are much higher now than was predicted at the start of the year. It means those remortgaging, possibly after the post-Covid boom in the housing market, are facing the prospect of higher mortgage payments.
Some people have been choosing to move onto tracker deals instead, taking a view - including some risk - of the Bank rate not moving towards a series of further hikes.
Get in touch
Do you have a mortgage, a credit card, a car finance agreement? How are interest rates affecting you?

title: How the midterms could fuel the K-shaped AI trade
titleJa: How the midterms could fuel the K-shaped AI trade
summaryJa: U.S. midterm results could slow data center development, raising the value of existing AI capacity while increasing pressure on debt-funded neoclouds.
bodyOriginal:
The U.S. midterms could widen the AI divide: tighter data center rules may reward tech giants with capacity in hand and squeeze debt-funded companies trying to catch up.
Democratic victories in key gubernatorial races raised the prospect of tougher scrutiny for data center projects, adding to investor concerns about how quickly new capacity can be built and financed.
In Texas, Democratic governor-elect Gina Hinojosa has proposed a statewide moratorium on new data center permits, although projects already under construction would reportedly be exempt.
As the markets digested the results on Wednesday, Microsoft and Amazon each surged more than 6%, while AI infrastructure provider CoreWeave plunged around 10%. Chipmakers Micron and Nvidia fell 7% and 3.17%, respectively.
Differences in borrowing costs are playing a key role in the split, James Sullivan, managing director and co-head of global fundamental research at JPMorgan, told CNBC's "Squawk Box Asia" on Thursday.
Sullivan said borrowing spreads have widened significantly for neocloud companies, leaving their cost of additional capital substantially higher than that of hyperscalers that benefit from more diversified customers and revenue streams.
"The fact that you're seeing this bifurcation in equity performance is largely driven by the view that existing capacity is significantly more valuable now because of incremental supply constraints," he said.
Data center risks
The midterm results could reinforce that view if they make new projects more vulnerable to permitting delays.
BMI warned that a sharp slowdown in data center construction and AI investment could produce a greater-than-expected decline in overall investment, The Business Times reported, citing the firm's post-midterm analysis.
The potential impact is uneven across the construction pipeline. Much of the data center capacity expected to come online in 2027 is already under construction, limiting the near-term impact of new restrictions.
Projects planned for 2028 face greater exposure to permitting delays and regulatory uncertainty, investment bank Nomura said in a note Wednesday about the midterm results.
Tighter regulations on data center construction could become a more significant headwind to AI investment from 2028, the firm said.
AI financing gap
Shares of Nvidia-backed neocloud CoreWeave, Nebius and Iren fell at least 30% in October, as tightening credit markets raised questions about how AI infrastructure projects would be financed. CoreWeave's five-year credit default swap spread has surged past 1,100 basis points, reflecting rising costs for investors seeking protection against a potential default.
The distinction may be how well companies can absorb delays and fund the capacity they do build. Hyperscalers have broader cloud businesses and more internally generated cash flow, while lower-rated neoclouds face greater exposure to borrowing costs, energy prices and refinancing conditions, JPMorgan Asset Management said in an Oct. 20 research note.
The asset manager said financially stronger hyperscalers could also secure cheaper capacity or acquire assets if weaker operators scale back.
